frame.p1Start: First of all, I'd like to find out a little about you.
frame.p2Start: In this part, each of you will get three pictures. I'd like you to talk about two of them on your own for about a minute, and then answer a short question about your partner's pictures.
frame.p3Go: Now, talk to each other about this question. You have about two minutes.
frame.p4Start: I'd now like to ask you both some more general questions.
frame.end: Thank you very much. That's the end of the test.

tests.title: Skills, teamwork and independence
tests.intro: Good morning. My name's Theo, and I'll be your examiner today. Your partner is Laura. Let's begin.

p2.studentIntro: Here are your pictures. They show people learning new skills in different situations. I'd like you to compare two of the pictures, and say what the people might find difficult about learning these skills, and how they might feel when they succeed.
studentQuestions: What might the people find difficult about learning these skills?
How might they feel when they succeed?

studentPhotos.alt: A young woman practising chords on a guitar, looking concentrated.
An older man at a computer class, with a teacher pointing at the screen.
A father holding the back of a bike while his daughter learns to ride.

p2.partnerQuestion: Laura, which of these skills do you think is the most useful to learn? Why?
p2.partnerAnswer: I'd probably go for the computer one, to be honest. These days so much depends on being able to get online, whether it's booking a doctor's appointment or paying bills. If you can't do that, you're at a real disadvantage. The guitar is lovely, but it's more of a luxury, isn't it?
p2.partnerIntro: Now, Laura, here are your pictures. They show people working together in different situations. I'd like you to compare two of the pictures, and say why the people might be working together, and how important it is for them to communicate well.
partnerQuestions: Why might the people be working together?
How important is it for them to communicate well?

partnerPhotos.alt: A team of surgeons and nurses during an operation.
A rowing crew pulling hard during a race on a river.
Colleagues sharing ideas in front of a whiteboard covered in notes.

p2.partnerLongTurn: Well, in the first picture there's a team of surgeons in an operating theatre, and in the second there's a rowing crew in the middle of a race. I suppose in both cases they're working together because the job simply can't be done by one person. The surgeons need each other's specialist skills, whereas the rowers need to combine their strength. As for communication, I'd say it's vital in both, but in different ways. For the surgeons, a misunderstanding could literally cost someone their life, so everything has to be extremely clear. The rowers, on the other hand, probably don't talk much at all during the race. They rely on rhythm, and on the person at the back calling out instructions. So communication matters more in the operating theatre, but in the boat, timing is everything.
p2.studentQuestion: Which of these situations do you think would be the most stressful to be in? Why?

p3.intro: Now, I'd like you to talk about something together. Here are some things that might help young people become more independent, and a question for you to discuss. First, you have some time to look at the task.
p3.question: How might these things help young people become more independent?
partnerLines: Shall I start? I think having a part-time job is a really good one, because you learn to deal with responsibility, and with people who aren't your friends or family. What do you think?
That's true. And what about living away from home? For me, that's where you really grow up, because suddenly there's nobody to sort things out for you.
I see what you mean. Travelling alone is interesting too, although I suppose it depends on the person. Some people find it a bit overwhelming at first.
Mm, I hadn't thought of it that way. Shall we talk about money? I think a lot of young people only learn to manage it when they have no choice.
Absolutely. And cooking... it sounds like a small thing, but it's actually quite a big step, isn't it?
p3.decision: Thank you. Now you have about a minute to decide which of these things would help young people become independent most quickly.
decisionLines: I'd say living away from home, because it includes most of the others. You have to cook, pay the bills and so on. Would you agree?
OK, fair enough. So shall we go for that one, then?

p4.q: Some people say young people today stay at home with their parents for too long. What do you think?
p4.partner: I think it's often not their choice, really. Rents are so high that it's almost impossible to move out before thirty in some cities.

p4.q: Is it better to learn from your own mistakes or from other people's advice?
Should schools teach practical skills like cooking and managing money?
p4.partner: I'd be in favour, as long as it doesn't replace the more academic subjects.

p4.q: How has technology changed the way young people become independent?
Do you think it's harder to become independent now than it was for your parents' generation?

tests.title: Relaxing, weather and communication
tests.intro: Good afternoon. My name's Theo, and I'll be your examiner today. Your partner is Marcus. Let's begin.

p2.studentIntro: Here are your pictures. They show people relaxing in different ways. I'd like you to compare two of the pictures, and say why the people might have chosen to relax in this way, and how relaxed they might feel afterwards.
studentQuestions: Why might the people have chosen to relax in this way?
How relaxed might they feel afterwards?

studentPhotos.alt: A woman reading a book on the grass in a sunny park.
Three friends on a sofa playing a video game, laughing.
A group of people doing yoga together in a bright studio.

p2.partnerQuestion: Marcus, which of these ways of relaxing would you choose? Why?
p2.partnerAnswer: Oh, definitely reading in the park. I spend most of my day in front of a screen, so the last thing I want when I'm trying to unwind is another screen. Being outside makes a big difference too, I find.
p2.partnerIntro: Now, Marcus, here are your pictures. They show people dealing with difficult weather. I'd like you to compare two of the pictures, and say what problems the weather might be causing, and how the people might be feeling.
partnerQuestions: What problems might the weather be causing?
How might the people be feeling?

partnerPhotos.alt: People hurrying along a city street in heavy rain, holding umbrellas.
A car stuck in deep snow on a country road.
People in a hot city square, fanning themselves in the sun.

p2.partnerLongTurn: Right. In this picture there are people struggling through heavy rain with umbrellas, and in this one a car seems to be stuck in deep snow. In the rain, I imagine the main problem is just getting soaked and maybe being late for work, which is annoying but not exactly dangerous. The snow looks much more serious. If that driver is stuck on a quiet road, they could be there for hours, and it might be getting dark. As for how they're feeling, the people in the rain probably feel fed up more than anything, whereas the driver could be genuinely worried, especially if there's nobody around to help. I guess the snow is the worse situation, partly because it's so unpredictable. You can always buy an umbrella, but you can't do much about a road that's completely blocked.
p2.studentQuestion: Which kind of weather do you find the most difficult to cope with? Why?

p3.intro: Now, I'd like you to talk about something together. Here are some things that have changed the way people communicate, and a question for you to discuss. First, you have some time to look at the task.
p3.question: What effect might these things have on the way people communicate?
partnerLines: Do you want to start with social media? I think it's made us communicate more, but maybe not better. What's your view?
Right. Video calls are an interesting one, because they're so much better than a phone call, but they still feel a bit artificial, don't they?
Working from home has changed a lot too. I think people miss those little conversations in the kitchen at work, which is where ideas often come from.
That's a good point. What about translation apps? They're amazing for travelling, but I wonder if they make people less motivated to learn languages.
And texting instead of calling... I have to admit I hardly ever phone anyone these days unless it's urgent.
p3.decision: Thank you. Now you have about a minute to decide which of these things has changed communication the most.
decisionLines: For me it has to be social media. It affects absolutely everyone, of every age. What do you reckon?
Yeah, I think we agree, then. Social media it is.

p4.q: Do you think people are losing the ability to have face-to-face conversations?
p4.partner: I wouldn't say losing it, but some people are definitely getting more nervous about it, especially on the phone.

p4.q: Should there be limits on how much time children spend on screens?
Is it ever acceptable to check your phone during a conversation?
p4.partner: Only if you explain why, I think. Otherwise it just comes across as rude.

p4.q: How might communication at work change in the future?
Some people say we share too much of our private lives online. What's your opinion?
